segments.translit: tam evārtha[ṃ] paramānandamudito hi kṛṣṇācāryaḥ pratipādayati—
segments.translation: Delighted by [supreme joy]{paramananda}, [Kāṇha]{p-kanha} sets out that same meaning:
segments.note: Munidatta introduces the song as [Kāṇha]{p-kanha}, delighted by [supreme joy]{paramananda}, setting out the same meaning again (cp.45.m1). The Tibetan has 'the meaning of reality' (de kho na nyid kyi don), perhaps a rendering of tam eva, 'that very', read as tattva.

flags.note: Where Munidatta has tam evārthaṃ, 'that same meaning' (cp.45.m1), the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has de kho na nyid kyi don, 'the meaning of reality'. De kho na can render tam eva word for word, so the translators may have read or construed it as tattva. The Tibetan also has rab tu tshim pa, 'fully satisfied', for mudita, 'delighted'.
The print runs muditohi together (cp.45.m1); read mudito hi, with the particle hi, which I leave untranslated.

segments.translit: manataru ityādi | anādibhavavāsanāpallavāśrayatvāt kṛṣṇācāryapādena svacitta[ṃ] taru(ra)tvena utprekṣitam | tasya cittataroḥ | pañcendriyeṇa śākhām adhimucya | āsā tasya patra(yantra)bahalaphalaṃ ceti |
segments.translation: 'The [mind]{citta} is a [tree]{tree}' and so on. Because it is the support of the shoots of the [habitual tendencies]{vasana} of beginningless [existence]{bhava}, [Kāṇha]{p-kanha} has pictured his own mind as a tree, by [poetic fancy]{utpreksa}. Of that mind-tree, he has [resolved]{adhimukti} on the five [senses]{indriya} as its [branches]{branch}. [Hope]{asa} is its abundant [leaves]{leaf} and [fruit]{phala}.
segments.note: Munidatta says [Kāṇha]{p-kanha} pictures his own mind as a tree because it supports the shoots of [habitual tendencies]{vasana} from beginningless existence; the five senses are resolved on as its branches, and hope is its leaves and fruit (cp.45.m2). The Tibetan has 'branches' for shoots and 'freed from' (grol ba) for adhimucya, 'resolving on'.

flags.note: Where Munidatta has adhimucya, 'having resolved on' (cp.45.m2), the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has grol ba, 'freed': de'i sems kyi ljon pa ni dbang po lnga'i yal ga las grol ba'o, 'that mind-tree is freed from the branches of the five senses'. The translators seem to have taken the root muc, 'release', at face value (or read vimucya). This reverses the sense; I follow the Sanskrit.

pañcendriyeṇa śākhām adhimucya (cp.45.m2) is an absolutive with no finite verb, and the instrumental singular beside the accusative is loose: literally 'having resolved on the branch with the five senses'. I take it as Kāṇha resolving on (firmly imagining) the five senses as the branches, as the song itself says (1a), and supply 'he has'.

The Tibetan of cp.45.m2 also has yal ga, 'branch', for pallava, 'shoot', so its mind-tree rests on 'branches of tendencies'; 'dod pa, 'desire', for āsā, 'hope', as in its line 1b; and 'bab pa, 'falling, flowing down', for bahala, 'abundant', as if from vah-, 'carry, flow' (compare the variant bāhā printed in line 1b).

In cp.45.m2 Shastri prints patra(yantra) and taru(ra)tvena. I read patra, 'leaf', which matches the song's pāta and the Tibetan lo ma; yantra, 'device', makes no sense here. tarutvena, 'as a tree', is the expected form.

segments.translit: dhruvapadena tasyānutpādaṃ sū(śū)cayati— varaguru ityādi | varaguruvacanakuṭhāreṇa tasya vāsanā chidyamānā satī kṛṣṇācāryo vadati sa eva cittatarur eva bhūmau punar notpadyate | tathā ca dvikalpe— na buddho labhyate 'nyate ityādi ||
segments.translation: With the [refrain]{dhruvapada} he indicates its [non-arising]{anutpada}. 'Excellent guru' and so on. When its [habitual tendencies]{vasana} are being [cut]{cutting} with the [axe]{axe} of the excellent [guru's word]{guru-vacana}, [Kāṇha]{p-kanha} says, that very [mind]{citta}-[tree]{tree} does not arise again in the ground. And so it says in the [Hevajra]{tx-hevajra}: 'A [buddha]{buddha} is not found elsewhere…' and so on.
segments.note: Munidatta says the refrain points to the mind-tree's [non-arising]{anutpada}: once its [habitual tendencies]{vasana} are cut with the axe of the excellent guru's word, that very mind-tree does not arise again in the ground (cp.45.m3). He adds the Hevajra's 'a buddha is not found elsewhere'. The Tibetan reads 'like the mind-tree' (bzhin du), as if iva for eva.

citations.quoted: na buddho labhyate 'nyate (for 'nyatra) ityādi: 'a buddha is not found elsewhere…'
citations.work: Hevajra Tantra (cited as Dvikalpa; Tibetan brtag pa gnyis pa)

flags.note: The quotation in cp.45.m3 reads 'nyate; the sense needs 'nyatra, 'elsewhere', which the Tibetan gzhan du confirms. In sū(śū)cayati, sūcayati, 'indicates', is the expected form.
tasya vāsanā chidyamānā satī (cp.45.m3) is nominative where a locative absolute (chidyamānāyāṃ satyām) is expected; the sense, 'while its tendencies are being cut', is clear.

The Tibetan of cp.45.m3 has de nyid sems ljon shing bzhin du sa gzhir slar skye ba med do, 'that itself, like the mind-tree, does not arise again in the ground', as if reading cittatarur iva for cittatarur eva. It adds nyams par byed, 'impairs', to the cutting, and has bla ma dam pa, 'true guru', for varaguru, 'excellent guru'.

segments.translit: dvitīyapadena guruvacanapravāham āha— bāṭai ityādi | so 'pi cittataruḥ svaśubhāśubhaṃ jalaṃ gṛhītvā sva[ya]m anādisaṃsārabhūmau vardhate | a[tha] śrīguruṃ pṛṣṭvā tasya vacanānubhavaṃ kṛtvā vidujaneti yogīndrās tasya cittavṛkṣasya chedaṃ kurvanti |
segments.translation: With the second [verse]{pada} he states the flow of the [guru's word]{guru-vacana}. 'Grows' and so on. That [mind]{citta}-[tree]{tree} too takes the water of its own [good and bad]{subhasubha} and grows by itself in the ground of beginningless [saṃsāra]{samsara}. Then, having asked the glorious [guru]{guru} and made his word their own [experience]{anubhava}, '[the wise]{vidujana}', that is, the [lords of yogis]{yogindra}, [cut]{cutting} that mind-tree.
segments.note: Munidatta says the couplet states the flow of the [guru's word]{guru-vacana} (the Tibetan has 'power', mthu): the mind-tree takes the water of its own good and bad and grows by itself in beginningless saṃsāra; then the wise, glossed as [lords of yogis]{yogindra}, ask the guru, make his word their experience, and cut it (cp.45.m4).

flags.note: guruvacanapravāha, 'the flow of the guru's word' (cp.45.m4), is an odd heading. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has bla ma'i gsung gi mthu, 'the power of the guru's word', and mthu regularly renders prabhāva; the translators apparently read guruvacanaprabhāvam, a word that looks much the same and one Munidatta often uses to introduce a couplet. I translate the print, 'flow'; 'power' may be the better reading.

guruparimāṇī (3b): Munidatta does not gloss the word (cp.45.m4). In its place he says what the wise do before cutting: they ask the glorious guru and make his word their own experience. His participles describe the wise, so this could unpack 'the wise who take the guru as their measure'; it equally describes cutting 'by the guru's measure', that is, by the guru's word as experienced. He does not decide between them. The Tibetan line's instrumental bla ma'i tshad kyis supports the draft's 'by the guru's measure'.

In cp.45.m4 the restoration sva[ya]m, 'by itself', is Shastri's. The Tibetan rang gi yid la sogs pa, 'one's own mind and so on', reads the unrestored svamanādi and lacks 'beginningless'. It also has 'khor bar byed, 'makes circle', for vardhate, 'grows', as if vartate, and a singular, 'the lord of yogis cuts his mind-tree'. a[tha], 'then', is supported by de nas.

The Tibetan of cp.45.m4 renders vidujana as rig pa dang ldan pa'i skye bo, 'people possessed of knowledge'. Its line 3b has mkhas pas dpyod pa, 'the learned examine', where the comment, like the Sanskrit, has cutting (gcod pa).

segments.translit: tṛtīyapadenāsampradāyayogināṃ saṃsāratām āha— jo taru ityādi | ye 'pi bālayoginaś cittavṛkṣasya chedam iti niḥsvabhāvīkaraṇaṃ na jānanti te 'pi saṃsāraduḥkhavāridhom̐ ṣaṭitvā(tvaṃ) patanti | punas tatraiva bhavagrahaṃ kurvanti | mokṣamārgaṃ na jānantīti |
segments.translation: With the third [verse]{pada} he states that [yogis]{yogi} who lack the [guru's lineage]{guru-sampradaya} remain in [saṃsāra]{samsara}. 'Whoever … the tree' and so on. Those [novice yogins]{balayogin} too who do not know the [cutting]{cutting} of the [mind]{citta}-[tree]{tree}, cutting meaning making it [without intrinsic nature]{nihsvabhava}, they too fall, rotting, into the [ocean]{ocean} of the suffering of saṃsāra. And right there they grasp at [existence]{bhava} again. They do not know the [path]{marga} of [liberation]{moksa}.
segments.note: Munidatta glosses [cutting]{cutting} as making [without intrinsic nature]{nihsvabhava}. Novice yogins lacking the guru's lineage, in place of the song's 'fool', do not know it; they fall into the ocean of saṃsāra's suffering and there grasp at existence again, not knowing the path of liberation (cp.45.m5). The Tibetan lacks the ocean and reads ṣaṭitvā as 'into the six realms'.

flags.note: ṣaṭitvā(tvaṃ) (cp.45.m5) is obscure; the print offers ṣaṭitvaṃ as an alternative. I take it as śaṭitvā, 'having rotted' (compare Sanskrit śaṭ-, 'decay', śaṭita, 'rotten'), echoing the song's saṛi, 'rotting', in 4b, just as patanti, 'they fall', echoes paṛiām̐. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has 'gro ba drug tu ltung bar 'gyur, 'fall into the six realms', taking ṣaṭ as 'six'.

The ocean (vāridhi) of cp.45.m5 is missing in the Tibetan translation, which has 'khor ba'i sdug bsngal gyis 'khor zhing, 'they circle through the suffering of saṃsāra', before 'fall into the six realms'. The print's vāridhom̐ stands for the locative vāridhau. The Tibetan renders asampradāya as man ngag dang bral ba, 'without the instruction'.

māṇai (4b): Munidatta's 'right there they grasp at existence again' (punas tatraiva bhavagrahaṃ kurvanti, cp.45.m5) stands where the song has bhaba māṇai, so he takes māṇai as holding to or taking up existence, which supports the draft's 'holds to existence'. The Tibetan line has srid par mos, 'is inclined to existence', and the comment srid pa len pa, 'takes up existence'.
The print's cittabṛkṣasya (cp.45.m5) is cittavṛkṣasya; Bengali script does not distinguish b and v.

segments.translit: caturthapadena mārgānuśaṃsām āha— suna taruvara ityādi | tasmād avidyāśūnyataro | bho bālayoginam iti | prakṛtiprabhāsvarakuṭhāreṇa gurusampradāyāt vāsanāṃ chedaṃ kuru | ḍālam iti | yena punar indriyasyādhīnaṃ na bhavatīti || 45 ||
segments.translation: With the fourth [verse]{pada} he states [praise]{anusamsa} of the [path]{marga}. 'The empty [fine tree]{taruvara}' and so on. Therefore, as for the tree empty of [ignorance]{avidya} — 'O' is addressed to the [novice yogin]{balayogin} — [cut]{cutting} its [habitual tendencies]{vasana} with the [axe]{axe} of natural [clear light]{prabhasvara}, through the [guru's lineage]{guru-sampradaya}. '[Branch]{branch}': so that it does not again fall under the power of the [senses]{indriya}.
segments.note: Munidatta cites 5a as suna taruvara, 'empty fine tree', like the Tibetan (shing mchog); the draft keeps the edition's su[na]taru. The novice yogin is to cut the habitual tendencies with the axe of natural [clear light]{prabhasvara}, through the guru's lineage, so the senses no longer rule it (cp.45.m6). The Tibetan says outright that the sky is natural clear light.

equations.en: so that it does not again fall under the power of the senses

flags.note: Munidatta cites line 5a as suna taruvara, 'the empty fine tree' (cp.45.m6), and the Tibetan line has stong pa'i shing mchog, where shing mchog renders taruvara. The edition prints su[na]taru, and the draft keeps it ('The empty tree'). Both witnesses support Shastri's restored [na]; neither supports taru without vara.

bho bālayoginam iti (cp.45.m6): an accusative with iti, 'the address is to the novice yogin', is awkward. The Tibetan has kye byis pa'i rnal 'byor pa nam mkha' zhes te rang bzhin gyis 'od gsal ba'o, 'O novice yogin! Sky means natural clear light.' That suggests a text like bho bālayogin gaganam iti prakṛtiprabhāsvaram, so bālayoginam iti may be bālayogin [gaga]nam iti with two syllables lost. This is my conjecture; I translate the print.

avidyāśūnyataro (cp.45.m6) is avidyāśūnyataroḥ before bho. I take the compound as 'the tree empty of ignorance', the usual sense of X-śūnya and of the Tibetan ma rig pa stong pa'i shing, and the genitive as going with the tendencies to be cut. It could instead be 'the empty tree of ignorance' (on song 28 he reads the fine tree as ignorance, cp.28.m4), and tasmāt could be 'from that (tree)' rather than 'therefore'; the Tibetan has de las.

mūla na ḍāla (5b): Munidatta cites only ḍāla and explains it as 'so that it does not again fall under the power of the senses' (cp.45.m6); he says nothing of mūla or na. Since the branches are the five senses (1a; cp.45.m2), he seems to take the branches as cut too, which suits 'neither root nor branch' better than the draft's 'at the root, not the branches'. The Tibetan line has no negative: shing de'i yal ga rtsa ba nyid nas gcod, 'cut the branches of that tree from the very root'.

The Tibetan of cp.45.m6 calls the couplet praise of 'the path of the guru's word' (bla ma'i gsung gi lam); renders gurusampradāyāt as bla ma'i gsung gi drin las, 'by the kindness of the guru's word'; cites 'with the axe' (sta re yis ni); adds yang dag par, 'rightly'; and lacks the citation ḍālam iti, though it keeps the explanation (dbang po'i dbang du mi byed pa).

questions: Line 5a: Munidatta cites it as suna taruvara (cp.45.m6), and the Tibetan line has stong pa'i shing mchog, 'the empty fine tree'. The edition prints su[na]taru and the draft keeps it ('The empty tree'). Both witnesses support Shastri's restored [na], and both read taruvara. Should 5a be redrafted with [fine tree]{taruvara}, or keep the edition's text and add a witness note?

Line 5b mūla na ḍāla: Munidatta explains only ḍāla, as 'so that it does not again fall under the power of the senses' (cp.45.m6). The branches are the five senses (1a; cp.45.m2), so he seems to treat the branches as cut too. That fits 'neither root nor branch' better than the draft's 'at the root, not the branches'; the Tibetan line has no negative ('cut the branches of that tree from the very root'). Should 5b get a meaning flag, or be redrafted?

cp.45.m4: the print has guruvacanapravāha, 'the flow of the guru's word'; the Tibetan bla ma'i gsung gi mthu points to prabhāva, 'power', one of Munidatta's usual words for introducing a couplet. Should the translation be emended to 'power', or keep 'flow' with the flag?

Line 3b guruparimāṇī: Munidatta does not gloss it. His paraphrase (ask the glorious guru, make his word one's own experience, then cut; cp.45.m4) fits both 'by the guru's measure' and 'the wise who take the guru as measure'. The Tibetan line's instrumental bla ma'i tshad kyis supports the draft. I suggest keeping the draft. Agree?

Line 4b māṇai: Munidatta's 'they grasp at existence again' (bhavagrahaṃ kurvanti, cp.45.m5) supports the draft's 'holds to existence'; the Tibetan line has srid par mos, 'is inclined to existence'. No change suggested.

cp.45.m6: I suggest that bho bālayoginam iti may have lost two syllables: bālayogin [gaga]nam iti, 'O novice yogin, sky means [natural clear light]'. The evidence is the Tibetan nam mkha' zhes te rang bzhin gyis 'od gsal ba'o. I translated the print. Should the conjecture go into a reader's note, or stay in the flags?

cp.45.m5: I rendered ṣaṭitvā as 'rotting', taking it as śaṭitvā, which echoes the song's saṛi (4b); the Tibetan reads 'six realms'. Is that acceptable, or would you rather leave the word marked as obscure?

Names: p-kanha's approved English is 'Kāṇha' and tx-hevajra's is 'Hevajra', and neither lists a variant, so I rendered Munidatta's kṛṣṇācārya(pāda) (cp.45.m1, cp.45.m2, cp.45.m3) as [Kāṇha]{p-kanha} and his dvikalpe (cp.45.m3) as [Hevajra]{tx-hevajra}. Should the commentary keep his own forms, Kṛṣṇācārya and Dvikalpa, as listed variants?

cp.45.m3 quotes only the opening of a Hevajra verse, na buddho labhyate 'nyatra. If it is the verse I believe it is (going on cittam eva hi saṃbuddho, 'the mind itself is the perfect buddha'), that continuation would explain why Munidatta cites it on the mind-tree. Please check the identification and give the verse number; I have not added one.
